```{r helpers, echo=FALSE}
# scientific workflow schematic; 'highlight' shades one box
draw_workflow <- function(highlight = NULL, cex = 0.9) {
  boxes <- c("PROBLEM", "THEORIES", "MODELS", "FIT", "COMPARE")
  subs <- c("what do we\nneed to know?", "candidate\nexplanations",
            "data-generating\n(process + noise)", "confront each\nwith data",
            "fit, prediction,\nrelevance")
  x <- seq(1, 9, by = 2)
  y <- 2
  w <- 0.8
  h <- 0.55
  shade <- function(lab) if (!is.null(highlight) && lab == highlight) "lightskyblue1" else "white"
  par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
  plot(NA, xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(-0.2, 4), axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
  for (i in seq_along(boxes)) {
    rect(x[i] - w, y - h, x[i] + w, y + h, col = shade(boxes[i]), lwd = 1.5)
    text(x[i], y + 0.18, boxes[i], font = 2, cex = cex)
    text(x[i], y - 0.22, subs[i], cex = cex * 0.75)
  }
  arrows(x[-5] + w, y, x[-1] - w, y, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  rect(6 - 0.7, 3.2 - 0.35, 6 + 0.7, 3.2 + 0.35, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 3.28, "DATA", font = 2, cex = cex)
  text(6, 3.0, "study design", cex = cex * 0.75)
  arrows(x[3], y + h, 6 - 0.7, 3.2, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  arrows(6 + 0.7, 3.2, x[4], y + h, length = 0.08, lty = 2, lwd = 1.2)
  segments(x[5], y - h, x[5], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  segments(x[5], 0.4, x[1], 0.4, lwd = 1.5)
  arrows(x[c(1, 2)], 0.4, x[c(1, 2)], y - h, length = 0.08, lwd = 1.5)
  text(6, 0.15, "REVISE the problem and theories; drop or down-weight poor models",
       cex = cex * 0.85, font = 3)
}

# heatmap of a covariance or correlation matrix (row 1 at the top)
show_matrix <- function(M, main = "", zlim = c(-1, 1) * max(abs(M))) {
  n <- nrow(M)
  pal <- colorRampPalette(c("firebrick", "white", "steelblue"))(101)
  par(mar = c(1, 1, 2, 1))
  image(seq_len(n), seq_len(n), t(M[n:1, ]), col = pal, zlim = zlim, axes = FALSE,
        xlab = "", ylab = "", main = main, asp = 1)
  box()
}
```

Packages: `mvtnorm`, `lme4`.

This material follows Bolker, *Ecological Models and Data in R*,
Chapter 9 (pp. 394-417), Appendix A.8 (pp. 484-485), and Chapter 10
(pp. 418-428).

# Standard statistics as likelihood models {#standard}

Regression, ANOVA, ANCOVA, and generalized linear models are usually
introduced as separate procedures with their own tables, tests etc. BUT, each one
is a data-generating model - a pretty simple one at that. We can write the
likelihood functions ourselves!

Here, we (1) play with fitting them both ways, (2) show how R turns a model formula
into a matrix, and (3) extend the idea to non-normal responses.

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-models, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("MODELS")
```

So far we have built *custom models*: pick a deterministic function, pick
a distribution for the noise, write the negative log-likelihood (NLL),
and minimize it. 

Bolker's Chapter 9 points out that the
procedures in an intro stats course are just special cases of the same procedure, with a 
linear deterministic component and (at least at first) a Gaussian noise component.

- `lm()` fits $Y \sim \text{Normal}(\text{linear function}, \sigma^2)$.
  Regression, ANOVA, and ANCOVA differ only in what goes into the linear
  function.
- In `glm()`, the expectation of the response is still modeled as a linear function 
  of the predictors, but on a different scale (defined by the 'link function'), and you can
  swap the Gaussian/Normal for another distribution.
- Both `lm()` and `glm()` assume every observation is **independent** after conditioning on the
  predictors. Later on this page we'll start relaxing the independence assumption (see
  [Modeling variance](#variance)).

Canned procedures are fast and well tested, so use them if you can (that is, if the key assumptions are met). 
But to know this, you need to understand the underlying model and its assumptions!
Packages for linear and generalized linear models are optimized, often
using closed-form solutions where possible. Custom likelihoods fit with
`optim()` are prone to errors and much slower. Canned models are still
limited, though, and it's very useful to be able to fall back on a
custom model when we need one.

## 2. WOD: linear or not? {#wod-linear}

The WOD (a short warm-up exercise at the start of class) listed several
models and asked which ones could reasonably be fit using `lm()` or `glm()`. 

In "linear model", 'linear' means linear **in the parameters**, not in the predictor $x$:

- $\mu = a + bx + cx^2$ is a curve, but each parameter enters as a
  simple linear coefficient times some pre-defined number. Rename $x^2$ as $w$ and it's
  multiple regression!
- $\mu = ax^b$ is nonlinear because $b$ is an exponent, not a simple linear 'slope' term. (Regressing
  $\log y$ on $\log x$ with `lm()` makes it linear, but that fit assumes
  multiplicative noise, not the additive Normal noise written here. A
  Normal GLM with a log link, $\log\mu = \log a + b\log x$, fits the model
  as written.)
- $\mu = \exp(a + bx)$ is nonlinear as written, but its log is linear (GLM with log link!).

More precisely, a model is linear in its parameters if the mean is a sum
of terms, each one parameter times a number computed from the data
alone:

$$\mu = \beta_1 z_1 + \beta_2 z_2 + \dots + \beta_k z_k$$

The $z$'s become the columns of the [model matrix](#model-matrix).

With a little creative transformation, every model in the WOD could be
fit with `glm()`. Linear and generalized linear models are more
flexible than they often get credit for.

## 3. The model underlying lm() {#lm-likelihood}

To explore this topic, here's an example (we'll use it throughout this week). 
Pinyon pine ring widths are a function of precipitation, where
wet winters tend to produce wider rings. We have increment cores
from 5 trees in each of 4 stands, with ring widths for 1996-2020 (25 years).
NOTE: these data are simulated, so the true model is known! 
Averaging the 5 trees in a stand gives one **chronology** per stand: 4 stands $\times$
25 years = 100 values.

Before we start with this example, it's important to recognize that 
averaging all the trees within each stand is a shortcut, and it isn't always a good one! It works here
because every stand has the same number of trees and no missing years.
But it throws away the variation among trees, and with unequal sample
sizes it would give a stand with 2 cored trees the same weight as one
with 20. Mixed models (see the [random intercept](#random-intercept)
section) can use each tree's measurements directly and estimate how
much trees within a stand differ.

```{r pinyon-data}
# pinyon ring widths (mm): 4 stands x 5 trees x 25 years; simulated
set.seed(21)
years <- 1996:2020
n_yr <- length(years)
precip <- round(rgamma(n_yr, shape = 9, scale = 22 / 9), 1)   # winter precipitation (cm)
stand_eff <- rnorm(4, 0, 0.12)
ar_dev <- matrix(0, 4, n_yr)            # shared year-to-year deviations within each stand
for (j in 1:4) {
  ar_dev[j, 1] <- rnorm(1, 0, 0.08 / sqrt(1 - 0.6^2))
  for (t in 2:n_yr) ar_dev[j, t] <- 0.6 * ar_dev[j, t - 1] + rnorm(1, 0, 0.08)
}
rings <- expand.grid(year = years, tree = 1:5, stand = LETTERS[1:4])
rings$tree_id <- paste0(rings$stand, rings$tree)
tree_eff <- setNames(rnorm(20, 0, 0.1), unique(rings$tree_id))
j <- match(rings$stand, LETTERS)
t <- match(rings$year, years)
rings$precip <- precip[t]
rings$width <- round(0.35 + stand_eff[j] + tree_eff[rings$tree_id] + 0.025 * rings$precip +
                       ar_dev[cbind(j, t)] + rnorm(nrow(rings), 0, 0.1), 2)

# stand chronologies: mean of the 5 trees in each stand and year
chron <- aggregate(width ~ stand + year + precip, data = rings, FUN = mean)
chron <- chron[order(chron$stand, chron$year), ]
head(chron)
```

```{r pinyon-plot, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.6}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
cols <- c("black", "steelblue", "firebrick", "darkorange")
plot(width ~ precip, data = chron, col = cols[as.integer(chron$stand)], pch = 19,
     xlab = "Winter precipitation (cm)", ylab = "Ring width (mm)")
legend("topleft", paste("stand", LETTERS[1:4]), col = cols, pch = 19, bty = "n", cex = 0.85)
plot(NA, xlim = range(years), ylim = range(chron$width), xlab = "Year",
     ylab = "Ring width (mm)")
for (s in 1:4) {
  sub <- chron[chron$stand == LETTERS[s], ]
  lines(sub$year, sub$width, col = cols[s], lwd = 2)
}
```

An ANCOVA (analysis of covariance) combines a grouping factor with a
continuous covariate. Its classic use is to ask whether groups differ
after accounting for the covariate: do the stands grow differently once
we account for the winter precipitation they all share? A usual first
check is whether the covariate has the same effect in every group
(parallel slopes). The model gives each stand its own intercept and
shares one precipitation slope:

$$\text{width}_{jt} \sim \text{Normal}(a_j + b\,\text{precip}_t, \sigma^2)$$

for stand $j$ in year $t$. Written as a custom likelihood:

```{r ancova-optim}
# ANCOVA: one intercept per stand (a[1:4]), shared slope b; sigma on the log scale
nll_ancova <- function(par, dat) {
  a <- par[1:4]
  b <- par[5]
  sigma <- exp(par[6])
  mu <- a[as.integer(dat$stand)] + b * dat$precip
  -sum(dnorm(dat$width, mu, sigma, log = TRUE))
}
chron$stand <- factor(chron$stand)
fit_ancova <- optim(c(rep(0.5, 4), 0, log(0.1)), nll_ancova, dat = chron,
                    method = "BFGS", control = list(maxit = 1000))
fit_lm <- lm(width ~ 0 + stand + precip, data = chron)   # 0 + : one intercept per stand

cbind(optim = fit_ancova$par[1:5], lm = coef(fit_lm))
c(optim = exp(fit_ancova$par[6]), lm = summary(fit_lm)$sigma)
```

The coefficients agree to several decimal places. The two $\sigma$
values differ slightly: the MLE divides the sum of squared residuals by
$n = 100$, while `lm()` divides by $n - 5$ to remove a small bias (the residual
degrees of freedom are $n - k$, where $k$ counts every coefficient: here
4 stand intercepts and the slope).

What `lm()` adds is speed and exactness. For a Normal linear model the
MLE has a closed form (see [Linear algebra](#least-squares)), so `lm()`
solves for it directly instead of searching (the lm() approach is much more 
computationally efficient!).

The classic ANCOVA tests are F-tests between nested models:

```{r ancova-tests}
fit_precip <- lm(width ~ precip, data = chron)
fit_slopes <- lm(width ~ 0 + stand * precip, data = chron)   # one slope per stand
anova(fit_precip, fit_lm)    # do stands differ, given precipitation?
anova(fit_lm, fit_slopes)    # same precipitation slope in every stand?
```

```{r ancova-numbers, echo=FALSE}
test_stand <- anova(fit_precip, fit_lm)
test_slopes <- anova(fit_lm, fit_slopes)
sd_stand_only <- summary(lm(width ~ stand, data = chron))$sigma
```

Stands differ strongly (F = `r round(test_stand$F[2], 1)` on 3 and
`r test_stand$Res.Df[2]` df), and the slopes test gives
p = `r round(test_slopes[["Pr(>F)"]][2], 3)`, close to rejecting even
though the true slopes are identical. Two cautions:

- Precipitation doesn't change the estimated stand differences here,
  because every stand had the same precipitation series. It only
  reduces the residual noise (residual SD
  `r f2(sd_stand_only)` without it, `r f2(summary(fit_lm)$sigma)` with
  it), which makes the stand test more powerful. A covariate shifts
  group means only when the groups differ in the covariate.
- The F-test treats the 100 stand-years as independent replicates of
  the stand differences. They aren't. Each stand's level partly reflects
  which 5 trees were cored, an error that repeats every year, and
  residuals are correlated from year to year. So the p-value overstates
  how sure we can be that the *stands* differ; the
  [random intercept](#random-intercept) and
  [AR(1)](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1) sections take
  this up.

> **Question:** Each precipitation value is shared by all four stands in
> a year. Does that matter for the independence assumption?

## 4. The model matrix {#model-matrix}

To fit a formula, R builds a **model matrix** $X$, with one row per
observation and one column per coefficient. The model is then

$$\mathbf{y} = X\boldsymbol\beta + \boldsymbol\varepsilon, \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2) \text{ independently}$$

Here are the rows for 1996 (one per stand) under two codings of the
same model:

```{r model-matrix}
rows_1996 <- chron$year == 1996
model.matrix(~ 0 + stand + precip, data = chron)[rows_1996, ]   # one column per stand
model.matrix(~ stand + precip, data = chron)[rows_1996, ]       # R's default coding
coef(lm(width ~ stand + precip, data = chron))
```

The default coding (**treatment contrasts**) has an intercept column of
1s, and its other stand columns are 0/1 indicators for B, C, and D. So the intercept is
stand A's intercept, and `standB` is how much B differs from A. The
fitted values are the same under either coding; only the meaning of the
coefficients changes.

- A factor with $k$ levels becomes $k - 1$ indicator columns plus the
  intercept.
- A continuous predictor becomes one column of its values.
- An interaction (`stand:precip`) multiplies columns together, giving
  each stand its own slope.

> **Question:** In a model with an intercept, why can't R include
> indicator columns for all four stands?

## 5. Generalized linear models {#glm}

A GLM keeps the linear predictor $\eta = X\boldsymbol\beta$ and changes
two things (Bolker 9.4):

- a **link function** $g$ connects the mean to the linear predictor,
  $g(\mu) = \eta$, so the mean (expected value of the response, after 
  accounting for predictors) stays in its allowed range;
- the Normal is replaced by another distribution (Poisson, binomial,
  Gamma, and others).

| Response | Distribution | Usual link | Mean |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| Counts | Poisson | log | $\mu = e^{\eta}$ |
| Successes out of $N$ | Binomial | logit | $p = 1/(1 + e^{-\eta})$ |
| Positive, right-skewed | Gamma | log (or inverse) | $\mu = e^{\eta}$ |

The second row (Binomial with logit link) might look familiar from
earlier in the course- it is also known as 'logistic regression'.
Here is the Poisson row, with simulated counts of cones on one branch of
each of the 20 trees, against each tree's mean ring width:

```{r cones-glm}
tree_means <- aggregate(width ~ stand + tree_id, data = rings, FUN = mean)
set.seed(5)
tree_means$cones <- rpois(20, exp(-0.5 + 3 * tree_means$width))

# Poisson GLM by hand: log(mu) = a + b * width
nll_pois <- function(par) {
  -sum(dpois(tree_means$cones, exp(par[1] + par[2] * tree_means$width), log = TRUE))
}
fit_pois <- optim(c(0, 1), nll_pois, method = "BFGS")
fit_glm <- glm(cones ~ width, family = poisson, data = tree_means)
cbind(optim = fit_pois$par, glm = coef(fit_glm))
```

Same answer again. `glm()` gets there by iteratively reweighted least
squares, which repeats a weighted `lm()`-style solve until it
converges. It's fast but limited to the specific families/links it knows.
Overdispersed counts need a negative binomial (`MASS::glm.nb()`), and
anything outside the list (a nonlinear mean, a mixture) needs a custom
likelihood (or use a different package that has already efficiently implemented your 
target likelihood).

## Discussion {#standard-discussion}

**Q1.** The ANCOVA residuals from consecutive years in the same stand
have a correlation of `r f2(mean(sapply(split(resid(fit_lm), chron$stand), function(r) cor(r[-1], r[-length(r)]))))`.
Which of the model's assumptions does that break? If we added year to
the model to test whether growth is declining, would you trust the
standard error `lm()` reports for that trend?

**Q2.** We treated stand as a fixed factor with its own intercept. A
manager wants to predict ring widths in a fifth stand that wasn't
sampled. What can this model say about it?

## Bonus: nonlinear least squares

When the mean is nonlinear in a parameter but the noise is still
Normal, `nls()` minimizes the sum of squared residuals by a
Gauss-Newton search (Bolker 9.3). That is the same as maximizing a
Normal likelihood with `optim()`, and it needs starting values too. For
example, a saturating response of ring width to precipitation:

```{r nls}
fit_nls <- nls(width ~ a * precip / (b + precip), data = chron,
               start = list(a = 1.5, b = 20))
coef(fit_nls)
```

# Linear algebra for statistics {#linear-algebra}

Before we start modeling variance (mixed models, spatial regression, time series models)
it really helps to have a little background in matrices (linear algebra).

When we start relaxing the independence assumption, we can no longer
multiply one likelihood per observation; we need the joint likelihood of
a whole set of correlated observations at once.

Models with structured variance are written with vectors and matrices.
This section covers several key matrix operations: multiplying, transposing,
inverting, and the determinant. It closes with the multivariate normal
distribution, which uses all these concepts. This section extends Bolker's
"cheater's guide" (Appendix A.8). For a visual introduction, see
3Blue1Brown's
[Essence of Linear Algebra](https://www.3blue1brown.com/?topic=linear-algebra)
videos.

## 1. Vectors and matrices

- A **vector** is a list of numbers, written in bold lowercase
  ($\mathbf{y}$, $\boldsymbol\beta$). By default a vector is a column.
- A **matrix** is a rectangle of numbers, written in uppercase ($X$,
  $V$). An $n \times p$ matrix has $n$ rows and $p$ columns. Element
  $x_{ij}$ is in row $i$, column $j$.
- In R, `matrix(1:6, nrow = 2)` fills a 2 $\times$ 3 matrix column by
  column; `dim()` gives its size.

```{r matrix-basics}
A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 0, 3, -1, 4), nrow = 2)
A
dim(A)
A[2, 3]     # row 2, column 3
```

## 2. Matrix multiplication

To multiply $A$ ($n \times k$) by $B$ ($k \times p$), take each row of
$A$ and each column of $B$, multiply them element by element, and add:

$$(AB)_{ij} = \sum_{m=1}^{k} a_{im} b_{mj}$$

The result is $n \times p$. The inner sizes must match ($k$); otherwise
the product doesn't exist. In R, use `%*%` (plain `*` multiplies element
by element).

The model matrix is the main use. Each row of $X\boldsymbol\beta$ is one
observation's predicted mean. With the default coding from
[the model matrix](#model-matrix), a stand C tree in a year with 30 cm of
precipitation has row $(1, 0, 1, 0, 30)$, so

$$\mu = 1 \cdot \beta_0 + 0 \cdot \beta_B + 1 \cdot \beta_C + 0 \cdot \beta_D + 30\,\beta_{\text{precip}}
= \beta_0 + \beta_C + 30\,\beta_{\text{precip}}$$

```{r xbeta}
X <- model.matrix(~ stand + precip, data = chron)
beta_hat <- coef(lm(width ~ stand + precip, data = chron))
mu_hat <- X %*% beta_hat               # 100 x 5 times 5 x 1 = 100 x 1
all.equal(as.vector(mu_hat), unname(fitted(lm(width ~ stand + precip, data = chron))))
```

Two habits from ordinary arithmetic fail for matrices:

- Order matters: $AB$ and $BA$ usually differ, and one of them may not
  even exist.
- Don't divide by a matrix. Multiply by its inverse instead (section 3).

## 3. Transpose, identity, and inverse {#least-squares}

- The **transpose** $A^T$ swaps rows and columns (`t(A)`). The inner
  product $\mathbf{x}^T\mathbf{x} = \sum_i x_i^2$ is a sum of squares, so
  the residual sum of squares is
  $(\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta)^T(\mathbf{y} - X\boldsymbol\beta)$.
- The **identity** matrix $I$ has 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere
  (`diag(n)`). $AI = A$, like multiplying by 1.
- The **inverse** $A^{-1}$ satisfies $AA^{-1} = I$ (`solve(A)`). Only
  square matrices can have one, and not all do. For a 2 $\times$ 2
  matrix,

$$\begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix}^{-1}
= \frac{1}{ad - bc}\begin{pmatrix} d & -b \\ -c & a \end{pmatrix}$$

The inverse doesn't exist when $ad - bc = 0$.

Minimizing the residual sum of squares (setting its derivatives to 0)
gives the **normal equations** and the least-squares estimate:

$$X^TX\,\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = X^T\mathbf{y}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta} = (X^TX)^{-1}X^T\mathbf{y}$$

For Normal errors this is also the MLE.

```{r normal-equations}
XtX <- t(X) %*% X
XtX                                      # 5 x 5
beta_ne <- solve(XtX, t(X) %*% chron$width)   # solves XtX beta = Xty
cbind(normal_eq = as.vector(beta_ne), lm = beta_hat)
```

> **Question:** Suppose $X$ also had an indicator column for stand A.
> What would go wrong when we call `solve(XtX)`?

`solve(A, b)` solves $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ without forming
$A^{-1}$, which is faster and more accurate. (`lm()` uses a related
method, the QR decomposition.)

## 4. Determinant and quadratic form

- The **determinant** $|A|$ (`det(A)`) is a single number for a square
  matrix. For 2 $\times$ 2 it's $ad - bc$. For a diagonal matrix it's
  the product of the diagonal. Geometrically, it's the factor by which
  $A$ scales areas (volumes, in higher dimensions); $|A| = 0$ means $A$
  flattens space and has no inverse.
- A **quadratic form** $\mathbf{x}^TA\mathbf{x}$ turns a vector into a
  single number. With $A = I$ it's the sum of squares.

The multivariate normal (MVN) density for a vector $\mathbf{y}$ of $n$
observations, with mean vector $\boldsymbol\mu$ and **variance-covariance
matrix** $V$, uses both (Bolker eq. 10.3.1):

$$f(\mathbf{y}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^n|V|}}
\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol\mu)^TV^{-1}(\mathbf{y} - \boldsymbol\mu)\right)$$

Compare the univariate normal,
$\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}\exp\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{2}(y - \mu)(\sigma^2)^{-1}(y - \mu)\right)$:

- $V^{-1}$ plays the role of dividing by $\sigma^2$.
- The quadratic form plays the role of the squared deviation.
- $|V|$ plays the role of $\sigma^2$ in the normalizing constant.

$V$ holds variances on its diagonal and **covariances** off it:
$V_{ij} = \text{Cov}(y_i, y_j) = \rho_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j$, where
$\rho_{ij}$ is the correlation. When the observations are independent
with equal variance, $V = \sigma^2 I$ and the MVN is a product of $n$
univariate normals:

```{r mvn-diagonal}
library(mvtnorm)
r <- resid(fit_lm)
sigma_mle <- sqrt(mean(r^2))
c(sum_dnorm = sum(dnorm(r, 0, sigma_mle, log = TRUE)),
  dmvnorm = dmvnorm(r, rep(0, 100), sigma_mle^2 * diag(100), log = TRUE))
```

(`emdbook::dmvnorm()`, used in Bolker's text, gives the same value.)

## 5. Valid covariance matrices {#valid-covariance}

Not every matrix can be a covariance matrix. It must be:

- **square and symmetric**: $\text{Cov}(y_i, y_j) = \text{Cov}(y_j, y_i)$;
- **positive definite**: $\mathbf{x}^TV\mathbf{x} > 0$ for every nonzero
  $\mathbf{x}$. Since $\mathbf{x}^TV\mathbf{x}$ is the variance of the
  weighted sum $\sum_i x_iy_i$, this says no combination of the
  observations can have zero or negative variance.

The practical check is that every **eigenvalue** is positive
(`eigen(V)$values`). Eigenvalues are numbers $\lambda$ for which
$V\mathbf{v} = \lambda\mathbf{v}$ for some vector $\mathbf{v}$: along
those directions $V$ only stretches. A correlation of $\pm 1$ gives an
eigenvalue of 0 (positive *semi*definite), and the MVN density no
longer exists.

```{r eigen-check}
V_ok <- matrix(c(4, 1, 1, 2), 2)       # variances 4 and 2, covariance 1
eigen(V_ok)$values
```

With $n$ observations a covariance matrix has $n(n+1)/2$ distinct
entries, far more than the data can estimate. Every model that follows
builds $V$ from a few parameters in a way that guarantees it is
positive definite.

## Tools for the lab

| Task | R |
|:--|:--|
| Matrix product | `A %*% B` |
| Transpose | `t(A)` |
| Identity matrix, or diagonal matrix from a vector | `diag(n)`, `diag(v)` |
| Inverse; solve $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b}$ | `solve(A)`; `solve(A, b)` |
| Determinant; eigenvalues | `det(A)`; `eigen(A)$values` |
| Model matrix from a formula | `model.matrix(~ f + x, data)` |
| MVN log density | `mvtnorm::dmvnorm(y, mu, V, log = TRUE)` |
| Random MVN draws | `MASS::mvrnorm(n, mu, V)` |

## Bonus: matrices as transformations

Multiplying a vector by a 2 $\times$ 2 matrix moves the point it
represents. The matrix

$$R_\theta = \begin{pmatrix} \cos\theta & -\sin\theta \\ \sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{pmatrix}$$

rotates by angle $\theta$, and a diagonal matrix stretches each axis.
The determinant is the factor by which the transformation scales areas:
1 for a rotation, the product of the stretches for a diagonal matrix.

```{r transform, echo=FALSE, fig.width=9, fig.height=3.3}
sq <- rbind(c(0, 1, 1, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0))
mats <- list("rotate 45 degrees" = matrix(c(cos(pi / 4), sin(pi / 4), -sin(pi / 4), cos(pi / 4)), 2),
             "stretch: diag(2, 0.5)" = diag(c(2, 0.5)),
             "shear: det = 1" = matrix(c(1, 0, 1, 1), 2))
par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(2, 2, 2, 1))
for (nm in names(mats)) {
  M <- mats[[nm]]
  plot(NA, xlim = c(-1, 2.2), ylim = c(-0.6, 1.6), asp = 1, xlab = "", ylab = "",
       main = sprintf("%s (|A| = %s)", nm, f2(det(M))))
  abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "grey85")
  polygon(sq[1, ], sq[2, ], border = "grey50", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
  tq <- M %*% sq
  polygon(tq[1, ], tq[2, ], border = "steelblue", lwd = 2.5)
}
```

# Modeling variance: random effects and autocorrelation {#variance}

Every likelihood so far has been a product over independent
observations. Trees in the same stand, or ring widths in consecutive
years, aren't independent. This part shows how a shared random group
effect produces a structured covariance matrix and fits it by maximum
likelihood. Correlation through time, and why these fits are harder
than anything we have done so far, are on the
[Week 12 page](Week12_MixedModels.html).

## 1. Big picture

```{r workflow-noise, echo=FALSE, fig.height=2.8, dev="png", dpi=250}
draw_workflow("MODELS")
```

A model has a process part and a noise part. We've spent most of the
course on the process part and kept the noise simple: one variance,
independent observations. Under independence the likelihood factors,

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(y_i \mid \theta), \qquad
\text{NLL} = -\sum_{i=1}^n \log f(y_i \mid \theta)$$

which is why nearly every NLL we've written ends in
`-sum(d...(..., log = TRUE))`. When observations are correlated, the
likelihood is a single joint density for the whole vector, and for
Normal data that density is the [MVN](#linear-algebra) with a
non-diagonal $V$. Modeling the variance means choosing a structure for
$V$ with only a few parameters.

Real data sets are rarely that tidy. The information in one
observation can bleed into others, usually "neighboring" ones in some
sense: the same block, or nearby in time or space. Wrongly assuming
independence (multiplying the likelihoods together) implicitly assumes
the data carry more information than they really do. The result is
confidence intervals that are too narrow, and possibly wrong
inferences.

For the rest of the course, we will consider cases where observations
are not independent, such as:

- mixed models: correlation within groups;
- time-series models: correlation between nearby times;
- spatial models: correlation between nearby places.

## 2. WOD: two cores from one tree {#wod-cores}

The WOD asked how precisely the mean of correlated measurements
estimates the stand mean. The tool is

$$\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)$$

For $n$ measurements with equal variance $\sigma^2$ and equal pairwise
correlation $\rho$, the variance of the sum is the sum of all $n^2$
entries of $V$: $n$ variances and $n(n-1)$ covariances. So

$$\text{Var}(\bar y) = \frac{n\sigma^2 + n(n-1)\rho\sigma^2}{n^2}
= \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\big(1 + (n-1)\rho\big)$$

Setting this equal to $\sigma^2/n_{\text{eff}}$ gives the **effective
sample size**, $n_{\text{eff}} = n/(1 + (n-1)\rho)$, the number of
independent measurements that would be just as precise.

```{r neff, echo=FALSE, fig.width=6, fig.height=3.6}
n_seq <- 1:30
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(NA, xlim = c(1, 30), ylim = c(0, 30), xlab = "Measurements (n)",
     ylab = expression(n[eff]))
rhos <- c(0, 0.1, 0.3, 0.8)
for (k in seq_along(rhos)) {
  lines(n_seq, n_seq / (1 + (n_seq - 1) * rhos[k]), lwd = 2, lty = k)
}
legend("topleft", paste("correlation", rhos), lty = seq_along(rhos), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

As $n$ grows, $n_{\text{eff}}$ levels off at $1/\rho$. Adding more
correlated measurements can't make up for having few independent
units.

The same idea is behind the [effective sample size of an MCMC
chain](Week9_MCMC.html#chain-checks). In a chain the correlation between
draws fades as the gap between them grows, rather than being equal for
every pair, so the formula is different, but the meaning is the same. A
random-walk Metropolis chain for the myxomatosis Gamma model kept 18,000
draws after burn-in, but its shape parameter had an effective sample
size of only about 43. A well-tuned chain for the germination posterior
got about 910 from 4,500 draws.

## 3. A random intercept {#random-intercept}

Take each tree's mean ring width over the 25 years: 20 numbers, 5 per
stand. Trees in the same stand share soil, slope, and local climate, so
they resemble each other. A **random intercept** model says so
directly:

$$y_i = \mu + b_{j(i)} + \varepsilon_i, \qquad
b_j \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma_b^2), \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim \text{Normal}(0, \sigma^2)$$

for tree $i$ ($i = 1, \ldots, 20$), where $j(i)$ is the stand tree $i$
grows in, with all the $b_j$ and $\varepsilon_i$ independent. Instead of estimating four stand intercepts, we treat the
four stands as a sample from a population of stands and estimate the
spread among them, $\sigma_b$.

Using $\text{Var}(X + Y) = \text{Var}(X) + \text{Var}(Y) + 2\,\text{Cov}(X, Y)$:

- $\text{Var}(y_i) = \sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2$
- two trees in the same stand ($j(i) = j(k)$) share a $b$:
  $\text{Cov}(y_i, y_k) = \sigma_b^2$
- trees in different stands share nothing: covariance 0

So $V$ is **block diagonal**: one 5 $\times$ 5 block per stand, with
$\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2$ on the diagonal and $\sigma_b^2$ elsewhere in the
block. The correlation between two trees in the same stand,
$\sigma_b^2/(\sigma_b^2 + \sigma^2)$, is the **intraclass correlation**.

In matrix form, $V = \sigma_b^2 ZZ^T + \sigma^2 I$, where $Z$ is the
20 $\times$ 4 matrix of stand indicators (the model matrix for
`~ 0 + stand`). $ZZ^T$ has a 1 wherever two trees share a stand.

```{r ri-matrix, fig.width=8, fig.height=4}
y_tree <- tree_means$width
Z <- model.matrix(~ 0 + stand, data = tree_means)
ZZt <- Z %*% t(Z)
V_ri <- function(sigma_b, sigma) sigma_b^2 * ZZt + sigma^2 * diag(20)
V_ri(0.12, 0.1)[1:7, 1:7]     # first stand's block, and the start of the next
```

```{r ri-heatmap, echo=FALSE, fig.width=7, fig.height=3.6}
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
show_matrix(V_ri(0.12, 0.1), main = "Random intercept")
show_matrix((0.12^2 + 0.1^2) * diag(20), main = "Independent, same total variance")
```

The NLL uses `dmvnorm()` with this $V$; optimizing the log of each SD
keeps both positive:

```{r ri-fit}
nll_ri <- function(par) {
  V <- V_ri(exp(par[2]), exp(par[3]))
  -dmvnorm(y_tree, rep(par[1], 20), V, log = TRUE)
}
fit_ri <- optim(c(mean(y_tree), log(0.1), log(0.1)), nll_ri, method = "BFGS")
c(mu = fit_ri$par[1], sigma_b = exp(fit_ri$par[2]), sigma = exp(fit_ri$par[3]))

library(lme4)
fit_lmer <- lmer(width ~ 1 + (1 | stand), data = tree_means, REML = FALSE)
fixef(fit_lmer)
as.data.frame(VarCorr(fit_lmer))[, c("grp", "sdcor")]
```

`lmer()` agrees. (By default it uses REML, a variant of maximum
likelihood that corrects the downward bias in variance estimates;
`REML = FALSE` gives the plain MLE.)

```{r ri-icc, echo=FALSE}
sb_hat <- exp(fit_ri$par[2])
s_hat <- exp(fit_ri$par[3])
icc <- sb_hat^2 / (sb_hat^2 + s_hat^2)
```

The estimated intraclass correlation is `r f2(icc)`: two trees from the
same stand are more alike than two trees from different stands.

> **Question:** The variance among stands is estimated from only four
> stands. How much would you trust $\hat\sigma_b =$ `r f2(sb_hat)`?

## 4. Autocorrelation and fitting {#ar1}

Correlation through time (the [AR(1) model](Week12_MixedModels.html#ar1)),
[why models with structured covariance are harder to fit](Week12_MixedModels.html#harder),
the [discussion prompts](Week12_MixedModels.html#variance-discussion)
for this part, and a [model with a random intercept and AR(1)
together](Week12_MixedModels.html#bonus-combined) are on the

## Bonus: integrating out a random effect {#integrating}

Where did $V = \sigma_b^2ZZ^T + \sigma^2I$ come from? The likelihood of
a random-effects model averages over the values the random effects
could have taken. For one stand,

$$\mathcal{L}_j = \int \prod_{i:\, j(i) = j} f(y_i \mid \mu + b)\, g(b \mid \sigma_b)\, db$$

the probability of the stand's data given $b$, weighted by how likely
each $b$ is. When both $f$ and $g$ are Normal this integral has a
closed form, and the result is the MVN with block covariance (Bolker
10.5.1). For a Poisson or binomial response it doesn't, so software
approximates the integral (the Laplace approximation in `glmer()` and
`glmmTMB()`, or numerical quadrature), or a Bayesian sampler draws the
$b_j$ along with the other parameters and skips the integral.
